cards.title: AI Code is Everywhere, Trust is Not: Your Chance to Build the Missing Link
cards.thesis: While new, powerful AI models like DeepSeek V4 Pro, Grok 4.6, and Qwen3.8-2.4T are constantly being released and adopted, builders are increasingly worried about the reliability of the code AI generates. Many are 'scared to ship' because AI code can 'silently break' or prove 'unreliable long term,' creating a clear demand for tools that can verify AI-generated output.

evidence.text: I am scared to ship because of the countless stories of AI code silently breaking, AI code not being reliable long term.
DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813: a new advanced AI model with high engagement.
Grok 4.6: another new AI model generating significant discussion and analysis.
Qwen3.8-2.4T: yet another powerful AI model being shared and discussed, highlighting the rapid pace of development.

cards.opportunity: Everyone's shipping with AI-generated code, but they're whispering about how it 'silently breaks' and isn't 'reliable long term.' The problem isn't generating code, it's trusting it. What if you built a lightweight service that acts like a 'second pair of eyes' for AI-generated code, automatically running quick reliability checks and flagging potential silent failures *before* it gets shipped? You could hook into popular AI coding tools like Cursor or Replit, giving builders the confidence they need to actually deploy.

cards.title: OpenAI's Linux Invasion: Time to Build for Power Users
cards.thesis: OpenAI just dropped official desktop versions of its ChatGPT and Codex AI tools for Linux, making it way easier for Linux users to access powerful AI assistance directly on their machines. This move brings AI closer to developers and power users who often live in their operating system's command line (a text-based interface for interacting with your computer), creating new opportunities for deeply integrated tools.

evidence.text: OpenAI has officially launched the Linux version of the ChatGPT and Codex desktop applications.
The ChatGPT Desktop (Codex Desktop) app is now available for Linux users.

cards.opportunity: OpenAI just dropped official desktop apps for Linux, which is cool for GUI users, but a ton of Linux developers live in their terminals. Nobody's built a slick command-line interface or a set of smart shell scripts that lets you pipe code directly from your local files into Codex and get AI suggestions back *without ever leaving your editor*. Ship a simple CLI wrapper that connects to the same underlying APIs and you'll own the 'AI-native terminal workflow' for Linux devs by next weekend.
